summary:
No Hidalgo-specific statute, enforcement pattern or documented incident affecting trans people is supported by the vetted sources for this record. The operative framework is Mexico's national one, under which legal gender recognition is set state by state.

As of March 2025, 22 of Mexico's 32 states had legislated an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition, two further states operate such a procedure in practice without having enacted it, six state legislatures have enacted nothing, and only seven states extend recognition to children. Human Rights Watch published these figures on 31 March 2025 while calling on the states without procedures to adopt them.

The Supreme Court of Mexico set binding guidelines for the states and extended the right to recognition to minors in 2022, and the Inter-American Court of Human Rights likewise requires a simple, accessible procedure. Where a state nonetheless has no procedure, Human Rights Watch documents the consequence as identity-document mismatch that drives discrimination in schools, medical clinics and the labour market, with incidents of that kind recorded in Guanajuato and Tabasco.

The Human Rights Watch and Community Center for Inclusion report of 6 March 2024 sets out what a silent state law means on the ground in Tabasco: without identity documents matching a trans person's gender, every document request or appearance under scrutiny carries a risk of violence, harassment and humiliation, and trans people are excluded from employment, health services, education and financial transactions. That report was written against the August 2023 murder of trans woman Karina Gómez in Villahermosa and against a national figure of more than 95% of homicides going unpunished in 2022.
tangentialFactors:
Formal rights and their enforcement diverge across Mexico. Analysis published by Caroline Beer on the LSE USAPP blog on 22 November 2024 found that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are rarely enjoyed in practice; Beer stated explicitly that her earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ people in Mexico are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Killings of trans people continue and have drawn public protest. The Associated Press reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening period of that year, including activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, which triggered LGBTQ+ outrage and street demonstrations. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that violence against trans people and the murder of LGBTI+ defenders had increased over the previous year. Transgender Europe monitoring recorded 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico from 2008 to September 2021 and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a total second only to Brazil's 100.

Mexico City's Congress approved the Paola Buenrostro law in July 2024, criminalising transfemicide; it is named for a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished, and activists quoted at the time described the measure as critical to their feeling safe in the capital. In 2024 the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded investigation of all LGBTI violations using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may reach alarming levels.
localsOnly:
Residents of Hidalgo are governed by whatever legal gender recognition procedure their own state authorities operate, and nothing in the sources establishes that Hidalgo has enacted one. The Supreme Court of Mexico's 2022 guidelines are binding on Hidalgo's authorities, and they extend recognition to minors.

The practical stakes for residents are documented in the Tabasco material: identity documents that contradict a person's lived gender close off employment, health services, education and financial transactions, and each request for a document or appearance before an official carries a risk of harassment. Nationally, more than 95% of homicides went unpunished in 2022, which shapes what protection is realistically available after an attack.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Hidalgo's legislature has enacted an administrative gender-recognition procedure, and whether Hidalgo authorities operate one in practice, is not established by the sources for this record; the national counts are reported without a state-by-state breakdown here.

No Hidalgo-specific incident of violence against a trans person, no Hidalgo court decision, and no Hidalgo health-care or facilities rule is sourced. The named incidents available (Villahermosa, Guanajuato, Mexico City, Tabasco) are drawn from other states and are cited as evidence of the national pattern, not of conditions inside Hidalgo.

The national impunity figure of more than 95% of homicides unpunished in 2022 is a national statistic and has not been disaggregated for Hidalgo.
